lessons.title: Case Study: Planning a Full Year of Advance Tax for a Salaried Investor With Side Income

body.text: Everything in this course comes together in one worked year. Nandini is salaried, owns a let-out flat, holds FDs and shares, and runs weekend workshops. She pays ₹2,36,964 of advance tax across four dates and ends the year with ₹1,008 of interest. The same year, handled carelessly, would have cost her ₹20,323.

children.text: This final lesson follows one taxpayer from April to March. Watch three things: how her estimate changes each quarter, how the timing relief treats her share sales differently from her workshop income, and how small the leftover interest is when the system is followed.
Nandini is 38, a product manager at a listed IT company in Bengaluru, and on the new regime for tax year 2026-27. Her employer deducts TDS on salary correctly. Everything else is on her.

children.text: In the first week of June, Nandini lists what she can see: salary, rent from the Hyderabad flat, FD interest at her deposit rates, and dividends based on last year's payouts. She has no share sales and no workshops yet. Tax on that picture is ₹5,52,864, and expected TDS is ₹4,32,900, leaving ₹1,19,964 of advance tax.

children.text: She rounds up and pays ₹18,000 on 10 June, five days before the due date.
August to September: A Share Sale Changes the Picture

On 12 August she sells shares for a short-term gain of ₹1,80,000, taxed at 20% plus cess with no TDS. Because the gain arose after 15 June, the timing relief means her June instalment is not tested against it. Her September estimate rises to ₹5,90,304 of tax, or ₹1,57,404 of advance tax. By 15 September she must have paid 45% of that, which is ₹70,832. She pays ₹52,832 on 9 September.

body.text: Nandini books the gain on 12 August and updates her worksheet the same week, not in March. That single habit is what keeps the relief available: it applies only if the tax on the gain is paid in the remaining instalments.

children.text: October to December: The Workshops Begin

In October she starts running paid weekend workshops, which will earn ₹1,80,000 of profit for the year after expenses. This is business income, so it gets no timing relief: the law expects it to have been estimated from the start of the year. Her December estimate becomes ₹6,46,464 of tax and ₹2,13,564 of advance tax. By 15 December she needs 75%, or ₹1,60,173, so she pays ₹89,341 on 9 December.

body.title: Try It: Nandini's December Payment
body.prompt: By 15 December, Nandini must have paid 75% of her revised advance tax of ₹2,13,564. She has already paid ₹70,832 across June and September. How much does she pay in December? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: 75% of ₹2,13,564 is ₹1,60,173. Subtracting the ₹70,832 already paid leaves ₹89,341. Each instalment tops you up to the cumulative percentage of your latest estimate.

children.text: January to March: The Last Gain and the Final Payment

On 20 January she redeems equity mutual fund units, realising a long-term gain of ₹3,05,000. After the ₹1,25,000 annual exemption, ₹1,80,000 is taxed at 12.5%. Her final tax is ₹6,69,864 and her advance tax for the year is ₹2,36,964. She pays the balance of ₹76,791 on 10 March, five days before the deadline.

body.title: Show me the math: why she still paid ₹1,008 of interest

children.text: Each instalment is tested against her final figures, with capital gains excluded until the quarter they arose. Her workshop income is business income, so it counts from the first instalment even though it started in October.

The June and September tests include the workshop profit she could not have known about. That is the price of income that arrives late and gets no relief, and at ₹1,008 it is small. Had she anticipated the workshops in June, even roughly, the interest would have been nil.

body.title: Quick Check: Why No Interest for the Share Sales?
body.question: Nandini paid nothing towards her August share sale before 15 September, and nothing towards her January gain before 15 March. Why did neither create interest for the earlier instalments?
options: Because capital gains are exempt from advance tax
Because the gains arose after those instalment dates, and she paid the tax on them in the next instalment
Because her employer's TDS covered them
body.explanation: Capital gains, dividends and casual income are excluded from instalments due before they arise, provided the tax on them is paid in the remaining instalments. She paid the tax on the August gain by 15 September and on the January gain by 15 March, so the relief applied. Her workshop income got no such relief, which is where her ₹1,008 came from.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Quarter That Matters
body.textWithBlank: In the return, capital gains and dividends are reported with a ___-wise breakup, so that instalments due before the income arose are not treated as short.
body.explanation: The quarter-wise breakup tells the system when each gain or dividend arose, which is how the timing relief is applied. Keep contract notes and dividend advices so you can fill it accurately.

body.title: Scenario: Nandini's Colleague Does It Differently
body.scenario: Vivek sits next to Nandini and has almost the same year: the same salary and TDS, the same flat, FDs and dividends, the same two share sales and the same workshop income, ending with the same advance tax liability of ₹2,36,964. He pays nothing in June, September or December. On 14 March 2027 he realises the deadline is near and pays ₹2,36,964 in one go.
body.prompt: What does Vivek owe in interest, and how does it compare with Nandini? What single change would have helped him most?
body.modelAnswer: Vivek escapes interest for not paying advance tax, because he paid 100% within the tax year and well before 31 March. But every earlier instalment was short. Using the same tests as Nandini, his June shortfall is 15% of ₹1,76,124, his September shortfall is 45% of ₹2,13,564 and his December shortfall is 75% of ₹2,13,564, each charged for 3 months, giving ₹792, ₹2,883 and ₹4,803. His March payment was on time, so nothing is charged there: ₹8,478 in total, against Nandini's ₹1,008. Had he waited until filing in July instead, interest for not paying advance tax would have added about ₹9,476 more. The single most valuable change is the September payment: revising after the August share sale and paying the cumulative 45% would have removed the largest of his three charges and protected December as well.

body.title: The System, in Six Steps
steps: Early June: list every income source, estimate the full year, subtract expected TDS, and run the ₹10,000 test
Pay 15% by 10 June and save the challan receipt
Log every capital gain, dividend and new income source on the day it happens, with its date
Early September and early December: rebuild the estimate from scratch and top up to 45% and 75%
Early March: finalise the estimate including March income you are confident of, and top up to 100% by 15 March
April onwards: reconcile challans and TDS in AIS and Form 26AS, file on time with a quarter-wise breakup of gains, and pay any small balance as self-assessment tax immediately

cards.definition: Tax paid during the tax year on income not fully covered by TDS. Liability under section 403 (old 207).
Advance tax applies when estimated tax after TDS and TCS reaches ₹10,000. Section 404 (old 208).
15%, 45%, 75% and 100% cumulatively by 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March. Section 408 (old 211).
May pay the whole amount by 15 March in one instalment. Section 58 and section 408(2).
Residents aged 60 or over with no business or professional income need not pay advance tax.
1% a month from 1 April when advance tax paid is below 90% of assessed tax.
1% a month on instalment shortfalls, 3 months each for June, September and December, 1 month for March. Floors of 12% and 36% for the first two.
Capital gains, dividends and casual income are excluded from instalments due before they arise, if their tax is paid in the remaining instalments.
0.5% a month on refunds of 10% or more of tax, from 1 April if you file on time. Taxable when received.
Estimate in June, revise at every due date, pay a few days early, and reconcile in AIS and Form 26AS.

points: Nandini owed ₹6,69,864 of tax on ₹40,20,000 of income, of which ₹4,32,900 came through TDS and ₹2,36,964 through advance tax
Her estimate was rebuilt four times, and each instalment topped her up to the cumulative percentage of the latest figure
Her August and January capital gains attracted no interest for earlier instalments, because she paid the tax at the next due date
Her workshop income, being business income, got no timing relief, which is the whole reason she paid ₹1,008 of interest
Doing nothing until filing would have cost ₹20,323 on identical income, ₹19,315 more
The system is simple: estimate in June, revise at every due date, pay early, and reconcile after the year ends
